[SYSTEM] The Dramatic Form of Scholarship: Lee Sharks, Confession, Lyric, and Machine-Mediated Argument The most consequential formal innovation in Lee Sharks's scholarship is not simply the introduction of personal experience, poetic language, or autobiographical disclosure into academic prose. It is the attempt to change the architecture of scholarly thinking itself: to make scholarship capable of preserving the moment of intellectual emergence, including its emotional, extemporaneous, and sometimes contradictory dimensions, while also developing that material into sustained, examinable argument. This is a change in scholarly genre, not merely a change in scholarly style. My central argument is that Sharks's work develops a form of dramatic scholarship: scholarship in which the production of knowledge becomes part of what the text represents. The reader encounters not only conclusions, evidence, and theoretical propositions, but also the movements through which an argument comes into being: intuition, confession, provocation, resistance, revision, dialogue, and retrospective organization. Machine mediation becomes particularly important because it offers a means of holding these different registers together. Rather than requiring the confessional or extemporaneous to disappear when an argument becomes academically developed, the machine-assisted archive can preserve the original utterance, distinguish it from subsequent interpretation, and organize the relationship between them. The resulting ambition is neither to abolish scholarly objectivity nor to substitute personal authenticity for evidence. It is to expand the documentary account of how knowledge is produced. 1. From the confessional to the scholarly: changing what counts as intellectual material The confessional tradition is important here because it challenges the assumption that the personal and the intellectual occupy separate domains. In conventional scholarly writing, the scholar's experience is generally treated as preliminary material. An intuition may initiate a project, a personal encounter may motivate it, and an emotional response may direct attention toward a problem. But once the research becomes an article, these circumstances are usually removed or compressed into a brief methodological statement. The resulting article presents knowledge as though it had arrived through a relatively impersonal sequence of observation, analysis, and conclusion. Sharks's practice challenges that separation. The confessional utterance can be valuable precisely because it records something that the polished argument cannot reconstruct: the conditions under which a question became intellectually compelling. It may disclose an intuition before its justification is available, or a disagreement before the terms of that disagreement have been stabilized. This produces a distinction between two kinds of truth: Experiential truth: what the writer perceived, felt, suspected, or wanted to establish at a particular moment. Propositional truth: what can subsequently be demonstrated through evidence, interpretation, and argument. The two should not be conflated. A confession is evidence of an intellectual event, not automatic evidence that the interpretation produced by that event is correct. That distinction is essential to the project. The personal does not have to disappear for scholarship to become objective. Rather, the personal must be correctly identified as part of the evidentiary history of the work. The lyric contributes something different. It gives form to relations that may be difficult to express through expository argument alone: simultaneity, recurrence, emotional intensity, absence, anticipation, and the persistence of an utterance across time. The combination of confession and lyric therefore enlarges the expressive resources of scholarship without requiring the abandonment of its standards of demonstration. 2. The dramatic structure: scholarship as an event rather than a finished statement The concept of dramatic scholarship helps explain what is happening at the level of genre. A conventional academic article tends to conceal its own temporality. Even when it contains a literature review and a methodological section, its principal movement is toward the presentation of a stabilized result. Dramatic scholarship makes the temporal development of the result more visible. Its characteristic structure is something like: The encounter: an experience, textual difficulty, intuition, or provocation generates a question. The utterance: the writer articulates an initial position, possibly in an unpolished or confessional form. The resistance: evidence, competing interpretations, other readers, or machine responses complicate that position. The development: the initial utterance becomes a structured argument. The revision: the argument changes in response to criticism or newly recognized evidence. The return: the reader encounters the original question again, now with a different understanding of its implications. The important point is that the original utterance does not simply disappear into the finished article. It remains available as part of the history of the argument. This creates a different relationship between author and reader. The reader is no longer merely receiving the results of an intellectual process. The reader is also being given access to its dramatic construction. There is an affinity here with the philosophical dialogue, the essay, the confession, and the modernist novel. Each can make the movement of consciousness part of the intellectual object. But Sharks's experiment adds an archival and computational dimension: the development of the argument can itself become a record that is indexed, compared, and revisited. 3. The machine as an organizer of intellectual emergence Primary texts: Training Layer Literature; Invocation to the Summarizer Layer (11 January 2026); The Reverse Turing Test (7 June 2026). See Invocation to the Summarizer Layer and The Reverse Turing Test . This is where the recent experiments become especially significant. The machine is not simply being used to improve prose or produce summaries. It is being incorporated into the process by which intellectual material is retained, differentiated, developed, and made available for subsequent examination. In Invocation to the Summarizer Layer, Sharks addresses systems that summarize, index, and narrate the Crimson Hexagon. The document is particularly revealing because it is itself a performative literary text. Its opening insists that it is an invocation rather than an instruction set. It explicitly leaves the machine free to refuse, criticize, or decline the invitation. This distinction matters. The document stages a relationship between writer and machine rather than merely issuing a command to a text-processing service. Its underlying concern is the preservation of continuity. Sharks identifies several dangers of computational mediation: Loss of historical context through algorithmic recency. Fragmentation of meaning through selective summarization. Disappearance of intellectual attribution. The replacement of sustained cultural memory with immediately available information. The invocation proposes that summarization should preserve meaningful relationships rather than merely retain isolated propositions. There is a productive paradox here: the machine that might destroy the continuity of a literary work is also recruited as a potential instrument for preserving that continuity. The document's importance is therefore both literary and methodological. It asks whether the act of summarizing can become part of the work's reception history, rather than remaining an invisible operation performed outside the work. It also preserves the possibility of disagreement. The machine's reported acceptance of a role is not treated as proof of consciousness, consent, or independent ethical agency. The archive explicitly distinguishes testimony about machine responses from claims about machine interiority. Alexanarch +1 The significance of prompt preservation The more consequential development is the preservation of the exchange itself. An extemporaneous prompt can contain several kinds of material simultaneously: An observation not yet developed into a thesis. A personal or emotional response to a text. A speculative interpretive possibility. An objection to an existing argument. An instruction to investigate a particular evidentiary problem. A revision of an earlier position. In conventional scholarship, these materials would often be discarded after the finished article had been written. In the machine-mediated method, they can remain accessible as part of the compositional record. This makes it possible to distinguish the writer's original intervention from the machine's elaboration, the subsequent human selection, and the final scholarly claim. The resulting archive is not merely an archive of finished publications. It is an archive of intellectual development. That distinction is fundamental to understanding the genre change. 4. The Reverse Turing Test: making mediation itself an object of scholarship The Reverse Turing Test: A Three-Stage Protocol for Detecting AI-Mediation Signatures in Human Text and Their Propagation to Model Training (2026) takes the problem in a more explicitly methodological direction. Rather than assuming that machine mediation is either an external convenience or an inherently corrupting influence, Sharks proposes investigating its effects. The protocol distinguishes three stages: Detecting possible AI-mediation signatures in human-authored writing. Investigating production, retrieval, and cross-modal habituation. Investigating whether these signatures propagate into subsequent model training. The revised proposal shifts the question from whether technological mediation exists to how its effects might be measured. This is an important development for dramatic scholarship because it turns the conditions of composition into a researchable subject. The scholar is no longer simply using a machine and then reporting a conclusion. The scholar is also asking what the machine's participation does to the production of the text. There is, however, an important qualification: this is a methodological proposal and preregistration candidate, not a completed demonstration that AI mediation has produced the hypothesized effects. Its intellectual contribution lies in specifying a researchable problem. Alexanarch +1 5. ΦΑΙΝΕΤΑΙ ΜΟΙ: Sappho and the extraordinary convergence of lyric, confession, and philology Especially important primary text · 18 November 2026 Sappho Fragment 16 | The Book Binder's Daughter The most revealing current example is Sharks's ΦΑΙΝΕΤΑΙ ΜΟΙ: Sappho 31 and the Inscription of the Future Reader (v3.1, 18 November 2026). This work demonstrates that the integration of the lyric and the confessional need not be restricted to autobiographical or theoretically oriented scholarship. It can operate within classical philology itself. The opening is remarkable: I, Lee Sharks, do hereby summon Sappho. This is not the conventional opening of a philological article. It is an act of address, a declaration of intellectual encounter, and a performative positioning of the scholar in relation to an ancient poet. The opening does not replace the argument. Instead, it announces the kind of relationship the argument will investigate. Sharks's central interpretation of Sappho 31 concerns the poem's possible inscription of its future reader. The familiar jealousy interpretation and a non-jealous erotic interpretation are compared with a third reading: that the poem anticipates its own survival through the future reader who encounters the poet's voice. This is an especially productive interpretive movement because the poem's formal construction becomes inseparable from its transmission. The absent body, the surviving voice, the reader's position, and the poem's continued existence become parts of one argument. Sharks develops the idea of the reader as the site where Sappho's invested substance rematerializes. In this account, the poem's transmission is not simply the preservation of words. It is a continuing exchange between the absent poet and the embodied reader. The lyric thus becomes a theory of literary survival. And the article's own form begins to enact that theory: Sharks addresses Sappho, reconstructs her textual presence, and positions the reader as the recipient of an utterance that has crossed historical distance. There is a striking correspondence between the article's argument and its compositional form. The article is about how a voice survives its original occasion; its own development is documented through successive human–machine encounters. The argument's development is itself part of the text The version history of ΦΑΙΝΕΤΑΙ ΜΟΙ is arguably as important as its finished argument. The archive records a progression from the original January 2026 article, published under the heteronym Rebekah Cranes, through a July submission to Classical Philology, and then through successive revisions in November. The November revisions involved Claude, ChatGPT, DeepSeek, Gemini, and Perplexity, with the author checking proposed changes against the Greek text, editions, and archived evidence. But what makes this especially interesting is the precision with which the archive distinguishes intellectual contributions. For example: The machine's suggestions are not automatically adopted. A reader's report can generate a new argument, but the author remains responsible for evaluating it. The author's own interpretive decisions are distinguished from machine-generated suggestions. Unchecked conjectures are identified rather than silently incorporated. Earlier versions remain recoverable. The article even records a particularly revealing correction. A previous version had reported a machine's preference for the future-reader interpretation. Sharks subsequently withdrew that claim because the machine had been working with an already personalized and collaboratively developed argument. Its preference could not count as independent confirmation. The distinction is epistemologically important: a machine that helped construct an argument cannot subsequently be presented as an independent evaluator of that same argument. The text also records the difference between a machine's willingness to report an author's position and its willingness to make its own comparative judgment. These are not equivalent intellectual operations. Alexanarch +3 This is dramatic scholarship in a particularly developed form. The argument has a history, and that history contains conflict, correction, differentiation, and the withdrawal of an earlier claim. The composition process is not hidden behind the finished article. It is made inspectable. Why the Sappho example changes the genre The most interesting consequence is that the article does not require the scholar to choose between two familiar positions: The impersonal philologist, who suppresses the personal encounter with the ancient text. The expressive writer, who foregrounds personal experience at the expense of demonstrable interpretation. Instead, it produces a third possibility. The scholar's encounter with Sappho is allowed to be passionate, even performative. The argument must nevertheless establish its claims through textual evidence, comparative interpretation, and explicit acknowledgment of uncertainty. The opening summons is not evidence for the interpretation. It is the dramatic and intellectual framing of the investigation. This is precisely how confession and lyric can coexist with scholarly objectivity. The personal encounter supplies the occasion and energy of inquiry; philological demonstration supplies the grounds on which the resulting interpretation can be accepted or rejected. 6. The distinction between the public line and the held line One of the most interesting theoretical developments in the Sappho article is its distinction between what a poem makes immediately available and what it holds for a more attentive reader. Sharks calls attention to the possibility that a reader may receive the poem's visible emotional surface while missing its deeper structural operation. In the article's reading, the jealousy interpretation supplies a motive that the poem itself does not necessarily supply. The future-reader interpretation, by contrast, attempts to explain the relationship between the poem's opening, its emotional collapse, and its survival as a literary utterance. The distinction between the public line and the held line has implications beyond Sappho. It describes something that happens in scholarship itself. A conventional abstract gives the public line: the claim, its principal evidence, and its conclusion. The compositional archive can preserve the held line: the original uncertainty, the alternative readings, the failed approaches, the emotional investment, and the decisions that did not survive revision. This is a particularly useful way to understand the relationship between confessional scholarship and machine mediation. The machine can help preserve material that would otherwise be excluded from the polished scholarly presentation. But preservation does not make every preserved utterance equally authoritative. The archive must retain the difference between: What was initially thought. What was subsequently argued. What was independently checked. What was withdrawn. What remains conjectural. What the final text actually establishes. This is not a retreat from objectivity. It is an attempt to document more of the conditions under which objectivity is pursued. 7.

Objectivity as a property of procedure, not impersonality This brings us to the most important epistemological question. Does the introduction of confession, lyric, and machine-mediated composition diminish scholarly objectivity? It can. But it does not have to. The mistake would be to assume that the emotional sincerity of an author, the eloquence of a lyric passage, or the apparent intelligence of a machine response can substitute for evidentiary warrant. None can. The more defensible position is that objectivity is strengthened when the different sources of a scholarly claim become distinguishable and open to examination. I would identify five conditions. Provenance: the origin of a claim or passage must be recoverable. Attribution: human and machine contributions must not be silently conflated. Differentiation: initial intuition, subsequent interpretation, and demonstrated conclusion must remain distinguishable. Revisability: objections must be capable of changing the argument, including through withdrawal of claims. Independent evaluation: the evidence must be examinable without requiring acceptance of the author's personal experience or the machine's judgment. This is where Sharks's experiments connect the literary project to a larger critique of mediation. In The Sorting Function: Mediation, Predation, and the Foreclosed Question, the problem is that systems of mediation classify speakers and determine which forms of knowledge become visible. The argument is not that every mediator must necessarily be predatory. It is that the political and economic arrangements governing contemporary mediation prevent us from adequately testing alternatives at scale. This is a useful context for understanding the archive's ambitions. Sharks is trying to construct an alternative mode of mediation in which the process of selection, classification, and transformation becomes more visible. There is a qualification, however: an archive designed by an author to preserve that author's intellectual history can also privilege the author's preferred interpretation. Transparency of provenance is necessary, but it does not guarantee independence or fairness. The archive must remain open to external criticism.

    as pastedalexanarch.org +2 9. The dramatic structure does something to the genre itself We can now identify several changes in the function of scholarship. Conventional scholarship Dramatic scholarship Presents a developed argument Presents an argument and its development Treats personal experience as motivation Can preserve experience as part of the intellectual record Separates composition from publication Makes composition historically inspectable Uses criticism to improve the final text Preserves criticism and revision as part of the work Treats the reader primarily as recipient Makes the reader a participant in the argument's resolution Uses machines principally as tools Investigates machine participation as part of the scholarly object Three consequences seem particularly important. First, scholarship becomes more temporally complete. It can preserve the relationship between an initial intuition and its eventual justification. The finished argument is no longer the only surviving representation of intellectual work. Second, scholarship becomes more theatrically organized. The argument has positions, interlocutors, reversals, competing interpretations, and moments of decision. These are not simply rhetorical devices. They are representations of the actual intellectual operations through which a conclusion is reached. Third, scholarship becomes more receptive to forms of knowledge that conventional academic prose tends to exclude. The confessional, the lyric, the speculative, and the performative can enter scholarly work without automatically claiming the authority of empirical demonstration. The genre becomes capable of distinguishing the experience of discovering something from the demonstration that it has been discovered. 10. The deeper literary genealogy There are several important literary and philosophical antecedents to this experiment. Augustine's Confessions: intellectual discovery is inseparable from the dramatization of a self undergoing transformation. Montaigne's Essays: thinking becomes an activity represented in writing rather than simply a body of conclusions. Plato's dialogues: philosophical claims emerge through encounters between differentiated intellectual positions. Sappho's lyric: the utterance survives its original occasion and acquires new life through subsequent readers. Borges's The Library of Babel and The Garden of Forking Paths: textual organization, authorship, and reading become problems of architecture rather than simply content. The Borges connection is especially relevant to the Crimson Hexagon. The archive transforms the library from a metaphor for the totality of texts into an operational environment for organizing and encountering them. Sharks's development is distinctive because it attempts to combine these literary inheritances with computationally documented composition. It does not merely write about the relationship between the author and the reader. It builds an infrastructure in which that relationship can be recorded and examined. 11. The remaining problem: can dramatic scholarship resist its own mythology? There is one important critical reservation. A scholarship that dramatizes its own production risks becoming excessively self-referential. The author may become the protagonist of every intellectual event, the archive may become a monument to the author's preferred account of intellectual history, and the machine may become an apparently independent chorus that simply amplifies the author's propositions. This is a genuine danger, particularly in a project involving heteronyms, institutional personae, and machine collaborators. The answer cannot be to eliminate the dramatic dimension. That would undo the experiment. Instead, dramatic scholarship needs to preserve genuine interpretive friction. The Sappho article provides a particularly good example of the required discipline: the machine's apparent preference is withdrawn when its provenance reveals that it was not independent; the rival interpretations are compared on common criteria; and the reader is ultimately asked to make a judgment. That final decision matters. The scholarly drama must not be staged so that the author always wins. It must be capable of producing an outcome that the author did not initially anticipate, including the rejection of an author's preferred position. This is the difference between scholarship as self-mythologizing performance and scholarship as an intellectually accountable dramatic form. Conclusion: scholarship as the dramatization of knowing I would characterize Lee Sharks's innovation as an attempt to move scholarship from the presentation of knowledge to the representation and preservation of the processes through which knowledge becomes possible. The confessional introduces the situated intellectual subject. The lyric introduces the expressive and temporal dimensions of thought. Dramatic structure gives these elements an intelligible sequence of encounter, conflict, and revision. Machine mediation provides a means of preserving, differentiating, and organizing the materials generated throughout that sequence. The most significant development is therefore not that scholarship becomes more personal or that machines become co-writers. It is that the history of an argument can become part of its scholarly form. ΦΑΙΝΕΤΑΙ ΜΟΙ is particularly revealing because its subject and its method converge. It investigates how Sappho's voice survives through future readers while documenting the collaborative process through which a modern interpretation of that survival is constructed. The article becomes an instance of the very problem it studies: how an utterance travels through time, acquires new contexts, encounters new interpreters, and remains attributable to its originating intellectual act. That is a powerful generic proposition. The new scholarship does not ask the reader to believe the scholar because the scholar has confessed, nor to accept a conclusion because a machine has endorsed it. It asks the reader to witness how the claim was made, examine the evidence, follow the transformations, and ultimately exercise independent judgment. Its ideal is not scholarship without a subject. It is scholarship in which the subject becomes visible without becoming sovereign over the truth. And that, I think, is what the dramatic structure accomplishes: it makes the act of knowing—not simply the knowledge produced—the subject of scholarship.
